title: Reading blood lactate
goal: Explain blood lactate as the balance of appearance and disappearance, read the shape of a lactate curve, and take a lactate sample that means something.

steps.title: A level set by in and out
steps.text:
Blood lactate is a balance: lactate released into the blood by some tissues ([rate of appearance](g:rate-of-appearance), Ra) against lactate taken up by others (rate of disappearance, Rd) [[c:ra-rd-balance]].

| Ra vs Rd | blood lactate |
|---|---|
| Ra > Rd | rises |
| Ra = Rd | stays flat, at any level |
| Ra < Rd | falls |

So a rise can mean more production, less removal, or both. And a flat line at 4 mmol·L⁻¹ isn't 'no production': it means large flows in and out are matched. As *Why lactate forms* showed, the level tells you little about how big the turnover is.

claims.text: Blood lactate concentration is the balance of lactate release into the blood and simultaneous uptake and removal; it does not show disposal rate.

evidence.quote: It is critical to understand that [La−]b represents a balance between La− production and release into the blood by various tissues versus simultaneous La− uptake and removal from the blood by other tissues.
blood lactate concentration is not an accurate indicator of lactate disposal and oxidation

steps.title: In minus out
steps.problem: During a steady 8-minute block, suppose lactate enters a runner's blood fast enough to add 0.60 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute, and removal takes away 0.45 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute. She starts at 1.5 mmol·L⁻¹. Where does she end?
steps: Net change per minute = Ra − Rd = 0.60 − 0.45 = 0.15 mmol·L⁻¹·min⁻¹.
End value = 1.5 + 1.2 = 2.7 mmol·L⁻¹. (A simplification: in real life Rd rises as the level rises, which is why lactate can level off.)

steps.title: The lactate curve at a glance
steps.text:
In a step test (power or pace raised every few minutes, a drop of blood at the end of each step), blood lactate traces a typical [curve](g:lactate-curve): close to resting values at first, then rising faster and faster. A shift of the whole curve to the right means better endurance [[c:curve-shape]].

Two bends matter [[c:two-breakpoints]]:

1. where lactate first rises above baseline;
2. the highest intensity at which production and removal still balance: the [maximal lactate steady state](g:mlss) (MLSS).

The lactate value at MLSS differs a lot between people, from about 1.5 to 7 mmol·L⁻¹ (average about 3.7) [[c:mlss-range]], so a fixed '4 mmol' threshold fits some athletes badly. The *Thresholds* module covers this in depth.

claims.text: In incremental exercise blood lactate rises gradually at first and then more rapidly; a shift of the curve shows a change in endurance capacity.

evidence.quote: In response to progressive, incremental exercise, [La(-)](b) increases gradually at first and then more rapidly as the exercise becomes more intense.
A shift of such lactate curves indicates changes in endurance capacity.

claims.text: The lactate curve has two typical breakpoints: the first rise above baseline, and the maximal lactate steady state.

evidence.quote: This model consists of two typical breakpoints that are passed during incremental exercise: the intensity at which bLa begin to rise above baseline levels and the highest intensity at which lactate production and elimination are in equilibrium (maximal lactate steady state [MLSS]).

claims.text: Blood lactate at MLSS ranges from about 1.5 to almost 7 mmol·L⁻¹ between individuals, averaging about 3.7.

evidence.quote: a wide range of [La−]b values at MLSS has been reported for different subjects, from as low as 1.5 mM to almost 7 mM. However, the average value is ≈3.7 mM.

steps.title: Where the drop comes from
steps.text:
Field tests use a drop of [capillary](g:capillary) blood from the earlobe or fingertip. The site can matter: in upper-body ski-ergometer work, fingertip values ran about 0.7 mmol·L⁻¹ higher than earlobe values [[c:site-diff]], while after rowing, in only 9 people, the toe, ear and fingertip did not differ significantly, though the fingertip still averaged up to 1 mmol·L⁻¹ higher [[c:site-same]]. Pick one site and keep it for every test.

Also check *what* your analyser reports. Whole blood holds less lactate than [plasma](g:plasma): on average about **70%** of the plasma value [[c:whole-plasma]]. A lab that reports plasma values will read higher than a device that reads whole blood, for the same sample.

claims.text: During ski-ergometer double poling, fingertip lactate was significantly higher than earlobe lactate (mean bias about 0.66 mmol·L⁻¹).

evidence.quote: Fingertip Bla values were significantly higher than earlobe values, with a mean bias of -0.66 mmol/L, reaching -0.86 mmol/L in the 4-8 mmol/L range.

claims.text: After submaximal rowing, plasma lactate from toe, earlobe and fingertip did not differ significantly in 9 rowers, although fingertip means were higher than earlobe means (6.36 vs 5.29 mmol·L⁻¹ at the lower load).

evidence.quote: No significant differences (p > 0.05) were found between any of the sites at either work intensity.
the mean (SD) plasma lactate concentrations sampled from the fingertip, toe, and earlobe were 6.36 (1.58), 5.81 (1.11), and 5.29 (1.24) mmol/l respectively

claims.text: Whole-blood lactate is on average about 70% of plasma lactate, at rest and in most exercise.

evidence.quote: At rest and during most exercise conditions, whole blood [La(-)] values are on average 70% of the corresponding plasma [La(-)] values

steps.title: Plasma or whole blood?
steps.problem: A lab reports a cyclist's plasma lactate as 5.0 mmol·L⁻¹. Her portable analyser reads whole blood. About what would it show for the same sample?
steps: Going the other way, divide by 0.7: a whole-blood 3.5 ÷ 0.7 = 5.0 mmol·L⁻¹ plasma. The 70% is an average, so treat the result as approximate.

steps.title: Analysers and timing
steps.text:
Portable analysers are good enough to track one athlete: their error is much smaller than the athlete's own biological variation. But compared with a lab reference, they tended to **under-read**, most at high values (about 15–23 mmol·L⁻¹) [[c:analyser-bias]]. Use the same brand of device each time.

Timing matters too. In a step test, sample at the end of each step. After an all-out effort of 30–120 s, blood lactate peaks at about 15–25 mmol·L⁻¹ only **3–8 minutes** later, and stays raised for over an hour [[c:peak-timing]]. A sample at the finish line misses the peak.

claims.text: Portable lactate analysers had analytical error much smaller than biological variation, but tended to under-read against a criterion analyser, especially at 15–23 mmol·L⁻¹.

evidence.quote: For all five portable analysers, the analytical error within a brand was much smaller than the biological variation in blood lactate (BLa).

Compared with a criterion blood lactate analyser, there was a tendency for all portable analysers to under-read (i.e. a negative bias), which was particularly evident at the highest concentrations (BLa ~15-23 mM).

claims.text: After all-out efforts of 30–120 s, blood lactate peaks at about 15–25 mmol·L⁻¹ some 3–8 minutes later and stays elevated for over an hour.

evidence.quote: In response to "all-out" maximal exertion lasting 30-120 seconds, peak [La(-)](b) values of approximately 15-25 mM may be observed 3-8 minutes postexercise.
As can be seen, peak [La−]b values typically appear at approximately 3–8 minutes postexercise, but [La−]b remains elevated for over 60 minutes.

points: Blood lactate is a level: it rises when appearance (Ra) beats disappearance (Rd), falls when Rd wins, and stays flat when they match, at any level.
A higher value can mean more production, less removal, or both; the level alone can't tell you which.
In a step test lactate stays low, then rises faster and faster; the two bends (first rise, MLSS) are covered in the Thresholds module. MLSS lactate ranges about 1.5–7 mmol·L⁻¹.
Keep the sampling site and device the same; whole blood reads about 70% of plasma; portable analysers tend to under-read high values.
After a 30–120 s all-out effort, lactate peaks 3–8 minutes later, not at the finish.

variants.stem: During a step test, a cyclist's blood lactate rises from 2 to 4 mmol·L⁻¹ between two steps. What does the rise tell you for certain?

options.text: Lactate entered the blood faster than it left
options.why: Right: a rise only means Ra exceeded Rd; it doesn't say which one changed.

options.text: Her lactate production doubled
options.why: The level doubled, but that could come from less removal as well as more production.

options.text: Her lactate removal stopped
options.why: Removal keeps going and usually rises too; it just fell behind appearance.

options.text: Her muscles ran short of oxygen
options.why: Lactate rises with glycolytic speed, not oxygen lack, in healthy exercise.

variants.stem: In the second half of a 10 km race, a runner's blood lactate keeps climbing. What can you say for certain?

options.text: Lactate is entering the blood faster than it is removed
options.why: Right: that is all a rising level shows for sure.

options.text: Her muscles make more lactate than at the start
options.why: Possible, but a fall in removal could give the same rise.

options.text: Her liver has stopped clearing lactate
options.why: Removal continues; it just isn't keeping pace.

options.text: Her legs have run out of oxygen
options.why: A rising lactate reflects the balance of in and out, not oxygen lack.

variants.stem: A cyclist starts a 10-minute block at 2.0 mmol·L⁻¹. Lactate enters her blood at 0.50 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute and is removed at 0.40 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute. What is her blood lactate at the end?

options.text: 3.0 mmol·L⁻¹
1.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This is the change only; it forgets the starting value of 2.0.

options.text: 7.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This ignores removal: 2.0 + 0.50 × 10.

options.text: 11.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This adds removal to appearance instead of subtracting it.

variants.solution: Net change = (Ra − Rd) × time = (0.50 − 0.40) × 10 = 1.0 mmol·L⁻¹. End = 2.0 + 1.0 = 3.0 mmol·L⁻¹.

variants.stem: A triathlete starts a 6-minute block at 1.2 mmol·L⁻¹. Lactate enters his blood at 0.80 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute and is removed at 0.65 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute. What is his blood lactate at the end?

options.text: 2.1 mmol·L⁻¹
0.9 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This is the change only; it forgets the starting value of 1.2.

options.text: 6.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This ignores removal: 1.2 + 0.80 × 6.

options.text: 9.9 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This adds removal to appearance instead of subtracting it.

variants.solution: Net change = (Ra − Rd) × time = (0.80 − 0.65) × 6 = 0.9 mmol·L⁻¹. End = 1.2 + 0.9 = 2.1 mmol·L⁻¹.

variants.stem: After intervals, a runner starts a 10-minute recovery jog at 3.0 mmol·L⁻¹. Lactate enters her blood at 0.40 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute and is removed at 0.55 mmol·L⁻¹ per minute. What is her blood lactate at the end?

options.text: 1.5 mmol·L⁻¹
4.5 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This flips the sign: removal is faster than appearance, so the level falls.

options.text: 7.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This ignores removal: 3.0 + 0.40 × 10.

options.text: 12.5 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This adds removal to appearance instead of subtracting it.

variants.solution: Net change = (Ra − Rd) × time = (0.40 − 0.55) × 10 = −1.5 mmol·L⁻¹. End = 3.0 − 1.5 = 1.5 mmol·L⁻¹.

variants.stem: A triathlete rides 30 minutes at constant power, and her blood lactate stays at 3.5 mmol·L⁻¹ throughout. What does that show?

options.text: Appearance and removal are matched, possibly both at high rates
options.why: Right: a flat level means Ra = Rd; it says nothing about how large they are.

options.text: Her muscles have stopped producing lactate
options.why: Production continues; it is matched by removal.

options.text: Her lactate removal has reached its limit
options.why: A steady level shows a match, not a maximum; above MLSS the level would keep rising.

options.text: She is above her highest sustainable intensity
options.why: Above MLSS lactate keeps rising; a flat level suggests she is at or below it.

variants.stem: At the same running pace, runner A's blood lactate is 2 mmol·L⁻¹ and runner B's is 4. A coach says: "B's muscles make twice as much lactate." What is the best judgement?

options.text: Unproven: B may make more, clear less, or both
options.why: Right: the level is a balance; without tracers you can't split production from removal.

options.text: Right: blood lactate directly measures production
options.why: Blood lactate is a level set by both production and removal.

options.text: Wrong: at equal pace production is equal, so B clears less
options.why: Production at a given pace differs between people, for example with mitochondrial content.

options.text: Right, because everyone clears lactate at the same rate
options.why: Clearance differs between people and rises with training.

variants.stem: In a step test to exhaustion, how does blood lactate typically change as power rises?

options.text: Near baseline at first, then rising faster and faster
options.why: Right: a slow start, then a steeper and steeper climb.

options.text: Rising in a straight line from the first step
options.why: The early steps barely change lactate; the curve bends upward later.

options.text: Rising fast at first, then levelling off
options.why: That is the reverse of the real shape.

options.text: Flat until exhaustion, then a sudden jump
options.why: The rise is gradual, then steeper; there's no single jump at the end.

variants.stem: A coach sets every runner's "threshold" pace where blood lactate reaches 4 mmol·L⁻¹. One runner's true MLSS sits at 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹. What is the likely result for her?

options.text: Her threshold sessions are set too hard, above her real steady state
options.why: Right: she reaches 4 mmol·L⁻¹ at a faster pace than her MLSS, so lactate would keep rising there.

options.text: Her threshold sessions are set too easy
options.why: 4 is above her MLSS lactate, so the pace that gives 4 is faster than her MLSS, not slower.

options.text: No problem: MLSS is at 4 mmol·L⁻¹ for everyone
options.why: MLSS lactate ranges from about 1.5 to 7 mmol·L⁻¹ between people.

options.text: No problem, as long as she is tested on a treadmill
options.why: The mode of testing doesn't fix a threshold that ignores individual differences.

variants.stem: A lab reports a runner's plasma lactate as 6.0 mmol·L⁻¹. About what would a whole-blood analyser show for the same sample?

options.text: 4.2 mmol·L⁻¹
8.6 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This divides by 0.7; whole blood is lower than plasma, so multiply.

options.text: 6.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This assumes plasma and whole blood read the same; whole blood is about 70% of plasma.

options.text: 1.8 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This takes 30% instead of 70% of the plasma value.

variants.stem: A cyclist's whole-blood analyser reads 2.8 mmol·L⁻¹. About what would a lab report as plasma lactate for the same sample?

options.text: 4.0 mmol·L⁻¹
2.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies by 0.7; plasma is higher than whole blood, so divide.

options.text: 2.8 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This assumes plasma and whole blood read the same.

options.text: 3.6 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This adds 30% (2.8 × 1.3); the right step is to divide by 0.7.

variants.stem: A lab reports a triathlete's plasma lactate as 4.0 mmol·L⁻¹. About what would a whole-blood analyser show for the same sample?

options.text: 2.8 mmol·L⁻¹
5.7 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This divides by 0.7; whole blood is lower than plasma, so multiply.

options.text: 4.0 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This assumes plasma and whole blood read the same.

options.text: 1.2 mmol·L⁻¹
options.why: This takes 30% instead of 70% of the plasma value.

variants.stem: A triathlete's spring lactate test used fingertip blood; the autumn retest uses the earlobe. At the same power, lactate is 0.6 mmol·L⁻¹ lower in autumn. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: The change may just be the switch of sampling site
options.why: Right: fingertip values can run about 0.7 mmol·L⁻¹ above earlobe values, as big as the change seen. Retest using one site.

options.text: Her endurance has clearly improved since spring
options.why: The change is no bigger than a known site difference, so it can't be read as fitness yet.

options.text: Earlobe blood can't be used for lactate testing
options.why: Earlobe sampling is standard; the problem is switching sites between tests.

options.text: Her endurance has clearly got worse since spring
options.why: Lower lactate at the same power would suggest better, not worse, endurance, and here the site changed anyway.

variants.stem: A track cyclist rides an all-out 1 km in about 65 s. When should you take blood to catch her peak lactate?

options.text: About 3–8 minutes after the finish
options.why: Right: after a 30–120 s all-out effort, blood lactate peaks 3–8 minutes later.

options.text: Right at the finish line
options.why: Lactate is still moving from muscle into blood; the peak comes minutes later.

options.text: In the last 10 seconds of the effort
options.why: Blood lactate is still rising then; it peaks well after the effort.

options.text: An hour later, once it has spread evenly
options.why: By then it is falling, though still raised; the peak has passed.

variants.stem: A runner's portable analyser under-reads high lactate values compared with a lab analyser. If her training zones are set from its readings, what is the risk?

options.text: Her ability is overestimated, so the zones come out too hard
options.why: Right: lower readings make each pace look easier than it is, so zones are placed at faster paces.

options.text: Her ability is underestimated, so the zones come out too easy
options.why: Under-reading makes lactate look lower, which makes her look fitter, not less fit.

options.text: No risk, because the analyser's error is random
options.why: The error was a tendency to read low, so it pushes the result one way.

options.text: Only her resting values are affected
options.why: The under-reading was largest at high values, not at rest.

variants.stem: A study tested six lactate analysers on 22 blood samples from 5 people, drawn and measured in a lab against a reference analyser. What most limits using its results for your field tests?

options.text: Few people, and lab samples rather than finger or earlobe drops in the field
options.why: Right: the authors note that field sampling from finger or earlobe may give slightly different results.

options.text: A reference analyser makes the comparison meaningless
options.why: A criterion method is exactly what you need to judge accuracy.

options.text: Measuring each sample several times hides the errors
options.why: Repeated measures are how reliability is estimated; they reveal errors.

options.text: None: lab results always carry over to the field
options.why: Sampling, handling and conditions differ in the field and can change readings.
